title: Guidelines on the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence for Judges and Judicial Officers and Support Staff of the Hong Kong Judiciary
author: Hong Kong Judiciary

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The Judiciary accepts selective, human-led deployment and adds a concrete judicial framework: assess each system’s capabilities and risks, preserve personal responsibility for decisions, verify outputs, and restrict high-risk legal analysis and sensitive-data use. This materially applies the cluster’s general proposition to court operations and judicial accountability.
qs: Before using any AI, it is important for the Court to understand and assess the AI’s capabilities and limitations, as well as address the potential risks involved.

JJOs should ensure that all judicial decisions continue to be independently and personally made by themselves, and should not under any circumstances allow generative AI to take over performance of their judicial functions.

st.t: AI filings: Disclosure rules divide otherwise similar courts
st.an: The Hong Kong Judiciary directly supports conditional AI assistance while retaining personal judicial responsibility. It requires verification before reliance, prohibits delegation of judicial decision-making, and adds confidentiality and task-specific safeguards. It does not resolve the cluster’s broader disagreement over filing disclosure regimes.
qs: JJOs should ensure that all judicial decisions continue to be independently and personally made by themselves, and should not under any circumstances allow generative AI to take over performance of their judicial functions.

JJOs and support staff must be mindful of the capabilities and limitations of the generative AI used and check and verify any information obtained to ensure its accuracy and reliability before using or relying upon it in their work.

st.t: Court governance: Assistive use retains human accountability
st.an: The Hong Kong Judiciary squarely supports the assistive, human-accountable model: generative AI may aid judicial work, but judges must personally make decisions, independently verify outputs and remain responsible for resulting materials. Its confidentiality, secure-device and breach-reporting rules also align with the cluster’s operational safeguards, while offering guidance rather than evidence of effectiveness.

st.t: Court responsibility: AI requires lifecycle supervision
st.an: The Hong Kong Judiciary directly supports lifecycle supervision: generative AI may assist court work, but judges must retain independent decision-making, users remain personally accountable for outputs, and accuracy, confidentiality and model limitations require continuing human oversight.
qs: JJOs should ensure that all judicial decisions continue to be independently and personally made by themselves, and should not under any circumstances allow generative AI to take over performance of their judicial functions.

While lawyers have a professional obligation to ensure that any material they present to the Court (however generated) is accurate and appropriate, JJOs should, in appropriate cases, remind individual lawyers of their obligations and confirm that they have verified the accuracy of any research done or case citations produced with the assistance of generative AI.

st.t: Generative automation: Fluent work product still needs authority
st.an: The Hong Kong Judiciary directly supports the cluster’s central proposition: generative AI may prudently assist judicial work, but authority, accountability and substantive decision-making must remain with the judicial officer. It also reinforces the need for model-specific understanding and accuracy checks, though it provides normative guidance rather than empirical performance evidence.
qs: JJOs should ensure that all judicial decisions continue to be independently and personally made by themselves, and should not under any circumstances allow generative AI to take over performance of their judicial functions.
It is important for a user to understand the features and limitations of the particular model being used.

st.t: Hallucination governance: Sanctions target inquiry failures
st.an: The Hong Kong Judiciary directly supports the cluster’s central proposition: generative AI may assist judicial and administrative work, but judicial functions and responsibility must remain human. It also endorses scrutiny and correction of outputs, verification of AI-assisted legal materials, protection of confidential inputs, and special attention to self-represented litigants’ limited verification capacity. It does not materially address sanctions doctrine or the dispute over mandatory AI disclosure.
qs: The above guiding principles can be succinctly summarised into the following two guiding rules –          Rule #1        :   Do not delegate judicial functions to AI.

While lawyers have a professional obligation to ensure that any material they present to the Court (however generated) is accurate and appropriate, JJOs should, in appropriate cases, remind individual lawyers of their obligations and confirm that they have verified the accuracy of any research done or case citations produced with the assistance of generative AI.

st.t: Judicial integrity: Controlled assistance replaces blanket bans
st.an: The Hong Kong Judiciary directly supports controlled, assistive AI use governed by judicial integrity. It permits technology to improve effectiveness and efficiency while requiring advance risk assessment and preserving judicial independence, impartiality, accountability and public confidence.
qs: Specifically, technology serves to support the Judiciary in performing its role and functions more effectively and efficiently, without compromising the principles of judicial independence, impartiality, and accountability.
In short, any use of AI by JJOs and staff must be consistent with the Judiciary’s overarching obligation to protect the integrity of the administration of justice.

st.t: Legal copilot: Verification costs define practical value
st.an: The guidelines directly support the copilot framing: generative AI may assist selected judicial tasks, but cannot replace personal judicial judgment. They also affirm that probabilistic limitations make human verification and accountability necessary, while offering no empirical evidence on whether verification preserves claimed speed or cost gains.

st.t: Machine judging: Accuracy cannot establish legitimate authority
st.an: The Hong Kong Judiciary accepts the cluster’s core distinction between technical capability or efficiency and legitimate judicial authority. It treats AI as support for judicial functions and makes its use subordinate to judicial independence, impartiality, accountability, institutional integrity and public confidence, rather than suggesting that accuracy alone authorizes autonomous adjudication.

st.an: The Hong Kong Judiciary directly supports the cluster’s supervised-aid model: generative AI may assist court work, but judicial functions remain personal and non-delegable. It does not provide evidence that verification consumes efficiency gains, but that omission does not undermine its clear support for the cluster’s principal proposition.

kp.k: AI must support, never replace, judicial decision-making
kp.d: The July 2024 guidelines permit prudent and responsible generative AI use for judicial and administrative work, subject to safeguards. They require judges and judicial officers to make decisions independently and personally: efficiency improvements must not compromise judicial independence, impartiality, accountability or public confidence. These are normative requirements, not findings about observed AI adoption.
qs: JJOs should ensure that all judicial decisions continue to be independently and personally made by themselves, and should not under any circumstances allow generative AI to take over performance of their judicial functions.

Specifically, technology serves to support the Judiciary in performing its role and functions more effectively and efficiently, without compromising the principles of judicial independence, impartiality, and accountability.

kp.k: Human verification is mandatory before relying on AI
kp.d: The guidelines warn that outputs depend on training, data reliability and prompts, may not draw on authoritative databases, and can remain inaccurate despite good prompts. Listed risks include fabricated authorities, incorrect legal information, factual errors and false assurances of accuracy. Judges and support staff must verify information before reliance; the document supplies no measured error rates.
qs: Beware that even with the best prompts, the output can be inaccurate, incomplete, misleading or biased.
confirm that the information is accurate if asked, even when it is not.

JJOs and support staff must be mindful of the capabilities and limitations of the generative AI used and check and verify any information obtained to ensure its accuracy and reliability before using or relying upon it in their work.
Using information generated without appropriate checking and verification risks causing injustice and damaging public confidence in the Judiciary.

kp.k: AI access requires institutional information-security safeguards
kp.d: Judges and support staff are directed to access AI through Judiciary-provided devices rather than personal devices, avoid untrusted networks and automatic connections to unknown WiFi, and use Judiciary email for work. These requirements constrain how AI may enter judicial workflows.
qs: In order to maintain information security, JJOs and support staff should only use information technology (“IT”) devices provided by the Judiciary (rather than personal devices which may not have proper safeguard on information security) to access the generative AI tools.
Do not connect IT devices provided by the Judiciary to untrusted networks (including WiFi), particularly those available at public places.
Use your Judiciary e-mail address in your work to maintain information security.

kp.k: Public chatbots must not receive protected information
kp.d: The guidelines warn that some chatbots retain inputs and reuse them in responses to other users. Unless using closed-end generative AI, users should assume inputs can become public. They prohibit entering private, confidential or sensitive information into open or public chatbots, require generalisation and anonymisation, recommend disabling available chat history, and direct users to refuse platform permissions giving access to device information.
qs: Unless you are using closed-end generative AI, it should be assumed anything you input can become publicly known.
JJOs and support staff should not enter any information which is private, confidential or sensitive into open or public generative AI chatbots.
Make sure that your input is adequately generalised and anonymised.
Disable the chat history function in the chatbots if this option is available.

kp.k: Existing privacy and intellectual-property obligations govern AI use
kp.d: The guidelines require compliance with Hong Kong's Personal Data (Privacy) Ordinance (Cap. 486), including its six Data Protection Principles. They also place responsibility for copyright and other intellectual-property compliance on users, warning that uploading protected published materials for summarisation or analysis could breach copyright and that outputs extracted from original works can raise copyright issues.
qs: JJOs and support staff should ensure compliance with the requirements under the Personal Data (Privacy) Ordinance (Cap. 486), including the six Data Protection Principles (“DPPs”)
For instance, uploading any published materials covered by intellectual property to a generative AI chatbot to obtain a summary or analysis could breach the author’s copyright.
Copyright issues may also arise from outputs that are extracted from an original work.

kp.k: Users must correct bias and retain personal responsibility
kp.d: The guidelines assert that generated responses reflect biases, geographical focus and misinformation in training data. Judges and support staff should make necessary corrections before reliance and remain personally responsible for materials issued in their names, even when using AI-derived information.
qs: will inevitably reflect any biases (including cultural or ethical biases) or geographical focus or misinformation in the training data.
JJOs and support staff should take note of this and make necessary corrections before using or relying upon the information generated.
JJOs and support staff should bear in mind that ultimately they are personally responsible for any materials produced in their name even where information derived from generative AI has been used.

kp.k: Courts should scrutinise AI-assisted submissions from court users
kp.d: The guidelines anticipate that lawyers and litigants-in-person may use AI to prepare litigation materials. Lawyers' existing accuracy obligations apply regardless of how materials are generated; judges should seek confirmation of verification in appropriate cases. The document warns that many litigants-in-person may lack the ability to verify AI legal information or awareness of its errors, and recommends enquiry about accuracy checks where AI use appears likely.
qs: While lawyers have a professional obligation to ensure that any material they present to the Court (however generated) is accurate and appropriate, JJOs should, in appropriate cases, remind individual lawyers of their obligations and confirm that they have verified the accuracy of any research done or case citations produced with the assistance of generative AI.
For litigants-in-person, many of them may not have the ability to verify the legal information provided by generative AI and may not be aware that such information is prone to error.

If it appears that generative AI may have been used to prepare submissions or other litigation documents, JJOs should make enquiry with the litigant, and ask what checks for accuracy have been undertaken.

kp.k: Potential uses centre on bounded supporting tasks
kp.d: The guidelines identify summarisation, speech and presentation preparation, legal translation and administrative drafting as potentially useful applications, rather than reporting measured productivity gains. Summaries must preserve accuracy and meaning; administrative drafting remains subject to warnings about retention and subsequent disclosure of entered data.
qs: Generative AI may potentially be useful in the following tasks
while AI tools are capable of summarising large bodies of text, care needs to be taken to ensure the summary is accurate and carries the same meaning as the original content;
AI tools can be used in planning a speech, producing an outline of potential speaking points and providing suggestions for topics to cover in a presentation;
Legal translation;

kp.k: AI is not necessarily a complete research substitute
kp.d: The guidelines require extra caution in legal research because chatbot coverage is limited by date range, jurisdiction and available types of legal materials. Whether a tool can reliably substitute for other research methods depends on its particular features and underlying database; the caution is qualified rather than an absolute prohibition on AI-assisted research.
qs: As generative AI chatbots are limited by the date range, jurisdictional reach, and types of legal materials they can access, using them for research requires extra caution.
Depending on the features of the AI model used and the underlying database, they may not be reliable as a complete substitute for conducting legal research using other means.

kp.k: Legal analysis is discouraged without proven safeguards
kp.d: The guidelines characterise probability-based generation without contextual understanding or critical examination of patterns as ill-suited to legal analysis because it can produce inaccurate or biased conclusions. Their recommendation against legal-analysis use is conditional: a model would need proven protection for confidential, restricted and private information and adequate built-in checking and verification to ensure accuracy and reliability.
qs: So long as the generative AI used generates text based on probability rather than an understanding of the nuances and context of any text, and does not have the ability to critically examine the patterns it identifies in data, it can result in drawing inaccurate or biased conclusions and is therefore ill-suited to legal analysis.
Unless there is a generative AI model with proven ability to protect confidential, restricted and private information
and adequate built-in checking and verification mechanism to ensure accuracy and reliability, using generative AI for legal analysis is not recommended.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The Hong Kong Judiciary frames generative AI as a potentially useful support tool, not a replacement for judicial decision-making.
pts.d: The guidelines identify potential uses in summarising information, preparing speeches and presentations, legal translation, and drafting administrative correspondence. Their augmentation-only approach is a normative requirement rather than a prediction of judicial automation: judges must personally make decisions and cannot delegate judicial functions. The source does not quantify efficiency gains or predict employment or legal-market changes.

pts.k: AI-assisted judicial work introduces accuracy and bias risks that require human verification before reliance.
pts.d: The Judiciary states that generative AI can fabricate legal authorities, misstate law, make factual errors and falsely confirm its own accuracy. It also attributes bias and geographical limitations to training data. It warns that unchecked reliance risks injustice and damage to public confidence, and requires users to check information and correct bias. These are qualitative risk claims, not measured error rates.

pts.k: Generative AI is not necessarily a complete substitute for conventional legal research and is conditionally discouraged for legal analysis.
pts.d: The Judiciary attributes research limitations to the date range, jurisdictional coverage and types of materials accessible to a chatbot. It describes probability-based generation without contextual understanding or critical examination as capable of producing inaccurate or biased conclusions. Legal analysis is not recommended unless a model has proven information protections and adequate built-in checking and verification mechanisms.

pts.k: Using generative AI can expose judicial information and create privacy and intellectual-property compliance risks.
pts.d: The Judiciary states that some chatbots retain inputs and use them in responses to others. It consequently requires a presumption of public disclosure outside closed-end systems, prohibits private, confidential or sensitive inputs into open or public chatbots, and prescribes secure devices and data handling. It also warns that uploading protected materials for summarisation or analysis, or using outputs extracted from original works, may raise copyright issues. These are conditional risks rather than findings that all AI systems disclose data or infringe copyright.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source offers institutional guidance, technical explanations and references to other authorities, rather than empirical performance evidence.
pts.d: The July 2024 guidelines explain risks through model training, probabilistic text generation, database coverage and information-retention practices. They reference guidance from courts in Canada, England, New Zealand and mainland China, alongside Hong Kong government and privacy authorities. Privacy and intellectual-property obligations are supported by references to Hong Kong legislation. No quantified productivity studies, model benchmarks, measured hallucination rates or named court-sanctions incidents are presented. The cited guidance is contextual authority, not demonstrated empirical validation of each claim.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The claims concern capabilities and risks as assessed in July 2024; future development is acknowledged without a forecast horizon.
pts.d: The Judiciary anticipates an increasing range of products but supplies no adoption timetable or date for reliable legal automation. Permissible use depends on the specific model, training data, prompts and safeguards. Summaries must preserve accuracy and meaning; legal research requires extra caution; legal-analysis use depends on proven confidentiality protections and adequate verification mechanisms. The prohibition on delegating judicial functions is categorical, not contingent on model improvement. The guidelines are intended to be updated as required.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Judges, judicial officers and support staff gain potential assistance but retain responsibility; lawyers and self-represented litigants face accuracy scrutiny, while the public bears justice-related risks.
pts.d: The primary subjects are Hong Kong judicial personnel performing judicial and administrative work. They must verify outputs, protect information and remain personally accountable for materials produced in their names. Lawyers remain professionally responsible for accurate submissions and may be asked to confirm verification of AI-assisted research or citations. The Judiciary warns that many litigants-in-person may lack the ability to verify AI-generated legal information or recognise its errors; judges should enquire about checks when AI use appears likely. The wider public is affected through potential injustice and damage to confidence in the administration of justice. The document does not claim that AI closes the justice gap.
